title: A listener registry read far more than written

blocks.text: The page's typical `CopyOnWriteArrayList` use is an **event listener registry**: listeners register rarely, events fire often, and a listener may change the registry while an event is being delivered. Its `addIfAbsent` refuses a listener that is already there.

Write the class `Listeners`, a registry whose listeners may change it while an event is being delivered. (The page's choice, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, also makes it safe to share between threads; the tests check the single-threaded rules below.)

items: `register(Consumer<String> listener)` adds the listener and returns `true`, or returns `false` if that listener is already registered.
`unregister(Consumer<String> listener)` removes it, returning whether it was there.

`fire(String event)` passes `event` to each listener registered **when the call began**, in registration order, and returns how many it called. A listener may call `register` or `unregister` from inside `fire`: a listener added that way hears only later events, and a listener removed that way does not stop the others from hearing this one.

cases.says: fire passes the event to every registered listener, in registration order, and returns how many it called.
Registering the same listener twice returns false the second time, and the listener is still called once per event.
A listener registered by another listener during fire is not called for that event, but is called for the next one.
A listener that unregisters itself during fire does not stop the listeners after it from being called.
When a removes b during fire, b still hears that event, because it was registered when fire began; it misses only later ones.

concepts: CopyOnWriteArrayList suits a listener registry: addIfAbsent refuses duplicates and notification iterates a snapshot that a listener may change without breaking it.
